pages.title: Hebrew and right-to-left
pages.description: Writing in Hebrew (and Arabic) in Lumen — direction per line, the interface in Hebrew, search that ignores niqqud and prefixes, spelling on this device, and exports that keep the direction.
pages.md:
Lumen is built for notes that mix Hebrew and English.

## The interface

`⌘K → Language: …` switches the interface. Hebrew and Arabic flip the
whole layout (sidebar, menus and dialogs mirror). The interface is in 8
languages: English, Hebrew, Arabic, Russian, French, German, Japanese and
Chinese.

## Direction in a note

- **Per line, automatically.** In the source editor each line takes its
  direction from its first strong letter: a Hebrew paragraph aligns right,
  an English one left, and the cursor and selection follow. Code blocks
  and the front matter are always left-to-right.
- **For a whole note:** put `dir: rtl` (or `ltr`) in its front matter.
- **For the editor:** `⌘K → Text Direction: RTL (Right to Left)` (and back
  with *Text Direction: LTR*).

## Search

Workspace search folds niqqud, final letters (ם/מ, ן/נ…) and the prefix
letters ו ה ב כ ל מ ש, so *בבית*, *והבית* and *הַבַּיִת* all find *בית*.
The exact form ranks first. See
[Workspace search](/workspace/search/). Links between notes and heading
anchors compare names the same way, so `[[שלום]]` finds *שָׁלוֹם.md*.

## Spelling, on this device

Hebrew paragraphs are checked **locally**: a final letter inside a word, a
repeated word, a space before punctuation. For spelling against a
dictionary, download Hspell's word list once with
`⌘K → Hebrew spelling: dictionary (download / remove)` (5.7 MB). It
is AGPL-3.0, so it isn't bundled; it is stored on this device, and the
same command removes it. Turn the check on with
`⌘K → Enable grammar check (LanguageTool)`. **Hebrew text never goes to
LanguageTool**: only paragraphs that are mostly Latin are sent, with any
Hebrew words in them blanked out.

## Exports

Exports keep the direction: Word (.docx) marks Hebrew paragraphs and runs
as right-to-left, and an exported HTML file opens right-to-left when the
note is Hebrew (or its front matter says `dir: rtl`).

pages.title: Legal citations (Israel)
pages.description: Rulings, laws, bills, books and articles by the Israeli uniform citation rules, and a citation from a case number in the note.
pages.md:
Lumen writes legal citations by **כללי האזכור האחיד בכתיבה המשפטית**, the third edition
(Tel Aviv University Faculty of Law, February 2021), which most Israeli law reviews and
faculties follow. Academic sources outside law use the
[Israeli APA style](/editor/citations/) ("APA 7 — Israeli academic").

## Insert a legal citation

Command palette → **Citations: legal source (uniform citation rules)…**. Choose the kind of
source, fill in the fields, and the citation is written as you type. **Insert** puts it at
the cursor, as plain text in the note, so it reads the same in the preview, in print and in
a DOCX or PDF export.

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| Supreme Court, printed | `בג"ץ 7/48 אל-כרבוטלי נ' שר-הבטחון, פ"ד ב 5, פס' 14 (1949).` |
| Lower court, printed | `ת"פ (מקומיים י-ם) 2857/85 מדינת ישראל נ' אורנן, פ"מ התשמ"ז(ג) 334 (1987).` |
| Unpublished (Nevo) | `ת"כ (תחרות) 745-07-18 בנק מזרחי טפחות בע"מ נ' הממונה על התחרות (נבו 28.11.2019).` |
| One judge's paragraphs | `בג"ץ 8300/02 נסר נ' ממשלת ישראל, פס' 35–36 לפסק הדין של הנשיאה (בדימ') ביניש (אר"ש 22.5.2012).` |
| Law | `חוק איסור נהיגה ברכב בחוף הים, התשנ"ז–1997, ס"ח 84.` |
| A section of a Basic Law | `ס' 10 לחוק-יסוד: הממשלה, ס"ח התשס"א 158, 159.` |
| Regulations | `תקנות הנמלים (תיקון מס' 3), התשמ"א–1981, ק"ת 956.` |
| Bill | `הצעת חוק ההתיישנות, התשס"ד–2004, ה"ח הממשלה 611.` |
| Book | `אהרן ברק פרשנות במשפט כרך שני: פרשנות החקיקה (1993).` |
| Article | `יפה זילברשץ "על חופש הביטוי המסחרי" משפט וממשל ג 509, חלקים ד(3)-(4) (1996).` |

- A **printed** ruling takes its report (פ"ד, פ"מ), volume, first page and year. Leave the
  report empty for an **unpublished** one, and give the database (נבו, אר"ש) and the date.
- The **Supreme Court** has no court in parentheses; every other court does.
- A **law**: type a date (`1997-03-05`) in the year field and the Hebrew year is filled in
  (התשנ"ז). A Basic Law is cited by its collection year instead.
- **Authors** are full names, separated by commas; Hebrew joins the last one with ו
  (אהרן ברק ובני שגיא).

## From a case number in the note

Put the cursor on a case number such as `ע"א 1234/05`, `בבג״ץ 7/48` or
`ת"א (מחוזי ת"א) 12345-06-19`, and run **Citations: legal citation from the case number at
the cursor**. The picker opens with the proceeding, the court and the number filled in;
the citation you insert replaces the number. Lumen knows the common proceedings of every
court: ע"א, רע"א, דנ"א, בג"ץ, ע"פ, רע"פ, בש"פ, עע"מ, ת"א, ת"פ, ה"פ, ת"צ, ע"ע, תמ"ש and more.
Prefix letters (בע"א, ובבג"ץ) and both quote marks (" and ״) are understood.

## Checked

`src/__tests__/legalCitations.test.ts` holds 20 golden legal citations: the rules' own
examples and the same rules applied to other sources. `israeliAcademicCitations.test.ts`
holds 20 academic ones in Israeli APA. The plan asks a law student to approve at least 38 of
the 40; that review has not been done yet.

pages.title: Markdown fidelity
pages.description: How closely Lumen follows the CommonMark and GFM specs, and the promise that opening and saving a file in either editor gives you back the same bytes.
pages.md:
A Markdown editor should never rewrite your files behind your back. Lumen is
tested against the official specs, and against its own round trip: open a
file, save it, and get exactly the bytes you started with.

## Spec conformance

Lumen's parser is tested against the official spec examples, which are kept
in the repository unmodified:

| Suite | Examples | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| CommonMark 0.31.2 | 652 | at least 99% |
| GitHub Flavored Markdown 0.29 | 670 (2 disabled upstream) | at least 98% |

The CommonMark parser underneath (micromark) passes every CommonMark example
on its own. What Lumen adds on top changes a handful of results on purpose:

| Where Lumen differs | Why |
|---|---|
| A leading `---` block is frontmatter | It holds the note's metadata (title, tags). The spec reads it as a thematic break and text. |
| A bare URL or email address becomes a link | GFM autolink literals are always on, including in examples that test plain CommonMark. |
| `ftp://` addresses are not linked automatically | Matches github.com today. Write `<ftp://…>` to link one. |
| Disallowed raw HTML (`<script>`, `<title>`, …) is not filtered by the parser | The preview sanitizes all raw HTML afterwards, which removes these tags. |
| A single line break inside a paragraph shows as a line break | The preview's soft-break setting. It is not part of the gated score. |

The GFM spec is pinned to CommonMark 0.29. Where CommonMark 0.31.2 changed the
expected result for the same input (mostly the emphasis rules), Lumen follows
the newer spec, and those examples are left out of the GFM score.

Any other failing example fails the suite, so every difference has to be
explained here.

## Round trip

Both editors are tested on more than 200 real Markdown files: everything in
the repository, Hebrew documentation included, and every section of the two
spec files. A CRLF copy of every tenth file is added on top.

- **Source editor:** open and save is byte-identical for every file. A file
  with Windows (CRLF) line endings stays CRLF. One with old Mac (CR) endings
  stays CR. In a file with mixed endings, the stray carriage returns stay
  where they are, shown as a special-character mark.
- **WYSIWYG:** unedited blocks are saved exactly as the file had them. An edit
  rewrites only the block you changed, such as the paragraph, list or table
  you typed in. Everything else keeps its own style: `*` or `-` bullets,
  `__bold__` or `**bold**`, table padding and blank lines. Blocks that WYSIWYG
  does not display, such as link reference definitions, are kept in place. A
  CRLF file gets CRLF in the blocks you add.

## Checking it yourself

```sh
npm run md:conformance
```

This runs the conformance suite, the round trip through both editors, and
the unit tests for the source-preserving save. The full results, with every
failing example and a per-file diff of the WYSIWYG serialization, are written
to `test-results/md-conformance/` and `test-results/md-roundtrip/`.

The spec files are © John MacFarlane and GitHub, Inc., under
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Their
source and commit are recorded in `src/__tests__/fixtures/md-spec/README.md`.

pages.title: Messages, empty states and undo
pages.description: How Lumen talks when something fails, when a panel is empty, and before it deletes anything — and the guide for writing those messages.
pages.md:
Lumen holds three promises about the moments people notice most:

1. **An error says what happened, what is safe, and what to do** — never a
   stack trace, an error code or a library's own words.
2. **An empty panel shows the way out**: one short sentence and one action.
3. **Nothing you made is deleted without a way back**: the action can be
   undone, or it asks first.

## Errors

Every error shown in the app goes through `explainError(e)`
(`src/lib/userError.ts`). It recognises the kind of failure and shows one
sentence for it, in the user's language; the raw text goes to the log, where
the AI doctor and a bug report can read it.

| Kind | What the person reads |
|---|---|
| no space | This device is out of storage space. Your text is still open here; free some space or export the vault, then try again. |
| permission | The browser did not allow this. Nothing was changed; allow access when it asks, then try again. |
| network | No connection. Your notes are safe on this device; try again when you are online. |
| timeout | This took too long and was stopped. Nothing was lost; try again, or try a smaller piece. |
| not found | The file is no longer there (moved or deleted). Nothing else changed; look for it in the trash or reopen it. |
| damaged file | The file could not be read: it is damaged or in another format. Nothing was changed; check the file and try again. |
| name taken | Something with that name is already there. Nothing was overwritten; choose another name. |
| AI busy | The AI service is busy (too many requests). Nothing was lost; wait a minute and try again. |
| no AI key, privacy policy, no local model | what was (not) sent, and where to change it |
| anything else | Something went wrong. Nothing you wrote is lost; try again, and if it happens again, the AI doctor and the log have the details. |

A cancel the person did themselves (closing a file picker, pressing Stop)
shows nothing. An error whose words are already written for the person
(translated, with what to do) is thrown as a `UserFacingError` and shown as
it is.

One exception is allowed: the syntax error of the person's **own** code or
diagram (Mermaid, Graphviz, PlantUML, ABC, SQL, a database block's query),
because its line and token are what they need to fix it. Each one is marked
`raw-error-allow` in the code.

## Writing a message (the guide)

- **What happened** — in the person's terms, not the program's: "The file
  could not be read", not "SyntaxError: Unexpected token".
- **What is safe** — say what did not happen: "Nothing was changed", "Your
  text is still open here", "Nothing was sent".
- **What to do** — one concrete next step: "free some space", "try again when
  you are online", "add a key in AI settings".
- No blame ("you entered an invalid…"), no codes, no exclamation marks, no
  "Oops". One or two short sentences.
- In Hebrew: plural address (נסו, בחרו) as in the rest of the app; the verb
  first ("שום דבר לא השתנה"); product and format names stay in Latin script
  (Ollama, WebGPU, ‎.zip).

## Empty states

Every empty panel — the file tree, search, outline, backlinks, tags,
comments, the graph, the trash, version history, templates, the audit log,
the privacy ledger, the AI panels — is an `` with one action:
*New note*, *Clear the search*, *Add a heading*, *Copy a link to this note*,
*Keep a version now*, and so on. The component's `action` is required.

## Destructive actions

Moving a note to the trash offers **Undo**; deleting from the trash for good,
emptying the trash, clearing the agent runs, deleting a comment, removing the
Hebrew dictionary, a git pull (which replaces files — and now moves files
deleted upstream to the trash instead of deleting them), applying the Vault
Doctor's link fixes and clearing the style profile **ask first**. A command
that deletes or replaces data declares `destructive: "confirm" | "undo"`.

## How it is checked

Three gates run in the unit tests (`src/__tests__/respectfulMessages.test.ts`)
and can be run alone:

```sh
node scripts/check-raw-errors.mjs     # 0 raw error texts on screen
node scripts/check-empty-states.mjs   # every empty state has an action
node scripts/check-destructive.mjs    # every destructive action asks or can be undone
```

pages.title: Editor modes
pages.description: Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG — pick the one that fits the task.
pages.md:
Lumen has four editor surfaces. Switch with `⌘1` / `⌘2` / `⌘3` / `⌘4`.

## Source (`⌘1`)

Plain CodeMirror 6 with markdown highlighting. Use it when you want to
write fast, see exactly what the file contains, or paste pre-formatted
markdown. The "Smart Insert" pill (`⌘⇧V`) is most powerful here.

**Best for**: writers who think in markdown; data-heavy notes where you
want the fence delimiters visible.

## Split (`⌘2`, default)

Editor on one side, live preview on the other. The split orientation
follows your viewport — horizontal on wide screens, vertical on phones.
Override via the **Scroll orientation** menu in the top bar.

Scroll-link is on by default — both panes track the same heading even at
different content heights.

**Best for**: most authoring sessions. You see the rendered output the
moment you type.

## Preview (`⌘3`)

Read-only render of the markdown. Tables, charts, diagrams, math, embeds
— everything in its final form. Print from here with
`⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`, which keeps the colours so PDFs come out
faithful.

**Best for**: reading notes back, proof-reading, sharing your screen.

## WYSIWYG (`⌘4`)

Notion-grade editing on top of Milkdown / ProseMirror. Slash menu (`/`),
inline math, drag-and-drop block reordering. Round-trips to plain
markdown — so a doc you wrote in WYSIWYG opens cleanly in Source.

**Best for**: visual thinkers; rich documents (presentations, decks);
anyone migrating from Notion.

## Toggle without leaving the keyboard

| Key | Mode |
| --- | --- |
| `⌘1` | Source |
| `⌘2` | Split |
| `⌘3` | Preview |
| `⌘4` | WYSIWYG |

The mode is remembered across reloads, so you come back to the view you
last used.

## Suggesting mode (track changes)

Turn it on from the command palette ("Turn on suggesting mode (track changes)") or with
the **Editing / Suggesting** pill in the status bar. While it is on, edits
in the Source / Split editor and in WYSIWYG are recorded as
[CriticMarkup](https://github.com/CriticMarkup/CriticMarkup-toolkit), so
the file stays plain markdown:

| You do | Stored as |
| --- | --- |
| Type text | `{++inserted++}` |
| Delete text (Backspace, Delete, cut) | `{--deleted--}` |
| Type over a selection | `{~~old~>new~~}` |
| Write a note by hand | `{>>comment<<}` / `{==highlight==}` |

- Typing next to your own insertion extends it, and consecutive deletions
  merge. Deleting text inside your own `{++ ++}` really deletes it.
- Undo / redo, edits from collaborators, and edits inside code blocks or
  inline code are never turned into suggestions.
- The editor shows insertions underlined in green, deletions struck
  through in red and comments highlighted; the preview renders them as
  `<ins>`, `<del>` and `<mark>`.
- Palette commands: accept / reject the suggestion at the cursor, accept
  all, reject all, next / previous suggestion. All of them work in
  WYSIWYG too; accept all / reject all also work from Preview.
- **In WYSIWYG** suggestions show as underlined insertions and struck-out
  deletions (hover for the author). Typing is recorded as an insertion,
  Backspace / Delete leave the text struck out and step over it, and
  typing over a selection becomes a substitution. Structural edits —
  joining two paragraphs with Backspace — aren't recorded as a
  suggestion and are undone; turn suggesting off for those.
- The status-bar pill shows how many suggestions the document contains.
- **Who suggested it.** When you are signed in, each new suggestion is
  followed by an author tag — a comment holding only `@name`, e.g.
  `{++new text++}{>>@Tal<<}`. The tag belongs to its change: accepting
  or rejecting the change removes it too. Hover a suggestion to see
  "Suggested by …"; the preview shows the name as a small comment.
  Typing inside someone else's suggestion keeps their name on it.

## TypeScript checks in code blocks

Run **Enable TypeScript checks in code blocks** from the command palette.
In the Source / Split editor, every ` ```ts `, ` ```typescript ` and
` ```tsx ` block (and JavaScript blocks, see below) is then checked by the
real TypeScript compiler:

- Errors get a wavy underline — hover it for the message (`TS2322: …`).
- Hovering a name shows its type (and its JSDoc, if any).
- Completions pop up while you type (after `.` or a few letters;
  `Ctrl-Space` forces them).
- Each block is checked on its own (its declarations don't leak into
  other blocks), in strict mode against the ES2022 and DOM libraries.
  Imports of npm packages aren't resolved and aren't reported.
- JavaScript blocks (` ```js `, ` ```javascript `, ` ```live-js `) get
  syntax errors, hover and completions; add `// @ts-check` as the first
  line to also get type errors.
- ` ```live-js shared ` blocks are checked together per scope
  (`shared=name`), in document order — a later block sees the names an
  earlier one declared, exactly as when they run. Re-declaring a name
  there is allowed.

The compiler (~1.3 MB compressed) runs in a background worker and is
downloaded only after you turn the setting on; it is not part of the
offline app shell. The setting is remembered.

pages.title: Obsidian syntax
pages.description: Callouts, comments, coloured highlights, footnotes with hover, math and image sizes, written the way Obsidian writes them, so a vault moves to Lumen without changing a line.
pages.md:
A vault that comes from Obsidian uses this syntax every day. Lumen reads it,
shows it in the preview and both editors, and saves it back without
changing it.

## Callouts

```md
> [!warning] Mind the gap
> The platform is curved.

> [!faq]- A question that starts folded
> Click the title to open it.
```

- Every Obsidian type works: `note`, `abstract`, `info`, `todo`, `tip`,
  `success`, `question`, `warning`, `failure`, `danger`, `bug`, `example`
  and `quote`, plus their aliases (`summary`, `hint`, `check`, `faq`,
  `caution`, `error`, `cite`, …). An unknown type looks like a note.
- `+` after the type makes the callout foldable and open, and `-` makes it
  foldable and closed.
- Without a title, the callout shows its type in your language.
- A Hebrew callout reads right to left, with its colour bar on the right.
- Callouts can be nested.

## Comments

`%%like this%%` is hidden in the preview, inline or across several
paragraphs. An unclosed `%%` hides the rest of the note, as in Obsidian.
The editors show comments faded, so you can still edit them.

## Highlights

`==text==` is highlighted. A colour emoji at the start picks the colour
(Obsidian 1.14): `==🔴urgent==`, and also 🟠 🟡 🟢 🔵 🟣. Highlights can
contain bold, italics and links, and they also work in table cells and
in Hebrew.

## Footnotes

`Text[^1]` with `[^1]: The note.` anywhere in the file. Hovering over or
tabbing to the number shows the footnote next to it, without scrolling to
the end of the note. Escape closes it.

## Math

`$inline$` and `$$block$$` math. The math renderer loads only when a note
contains math, so it never slows down opening the app.

## Images and their size

| Written | Shows |
|---|---|
| `![[photo.png]]` | the image |
| `![[photo.png\|300]]` | 300 pixels wide |
| `![[photo.png\|640x360]]` | 640 × 360 |
| `![[photo.png\|A cat\|200]]` | with alt text, 200 wide |
| `![A cat\|200](photo.png)` | the Markdown form, 200 wide |

In the preview, drag an image's edge (the right edge in English, the left
in Hebrew) to resize it. The new width is written into the note, as in
Obsidian 1.12.

## Tested

Forty golden notes covering all of the above, in English and Hebrew, are
rendered on every test run and checked element by element. They are also
part of the [round-trip corpus](/editor/markdown-fidelity/), so both editors
must save them byte for byte.

pages.title: Outline mode and block operations
pages.description: Fold headings and lists, zoom into one block, and move, indent, duplicate or delete whole blocks — on a plain Markdown file, in both editors.
pages.md:
Logseq, Tana and Workflowy made writing in an outline its own way of
working. Lumen gives you the same moves on an ordinary Markdown note: the
file stays plain Markdown, with nothing added to it.

## What a block is

- A **heading** together with its section: everything up to the next heading
  of the same or a higher level.
- A **list item** together with its children: the lines indented under it.
- Any other top-level block: a paragraph, a code block, a table, a quote.

Code is never structure: a `# line` or a `- line` inside a fenced code block
is left alone.

## The operations

They work the same in the source editor and in WYSIWYG, and in Hebrew
(right to left) as in English. Each is also in the command palette, under
**Outline: …**.

| Operation | Keys (Windows / Linux) | macOS |
|---|---|---|
| Move block up / down | Alt+Shift+↑ / ↓ | ⌥⇧↑ / ↓ |
| Indent / outdent | Ctrl+Alt+→ / ← | ⌘⌥→ / ← |
| Duplicate block | Alt+Shift+D | ⌥⇧D |
| Delete block | Alt+Shift+Backspace | ⌥⇧⌫ |
| Fold / unfold | Ctrl+Alt+↑ / ↓ | ⌘⌥↑ / ↓ |
| Zoom into the block / zoom out | Ctrl+Alt+Enter (Escape zooms out) | ⌘⌥↵ |
| Fold all / unfold all | palette | palette |

- **Moving** swaps the block with its neighbour at the same level, and the
  blank lines stay where they were. A heading moves with its whole section;
  a list item moves with its children. The first child of a section or a list
  doesn't leave its parent.
- **Indenting** a list item makes it the last child of the item before it;
  outdenting lifts it one level. Indenting a heading demotes its whole
  section (`#` → `##`, and every sub-heading with it).
- **In a right-to-left line the arrows follow the text**: the arrow that
  points to the line's end indents. In Hebrew that is Ctrl+Alt+←.
- **Zoom** shows only the block and its children, with a bar that takes you
  back to the whole note.

Drag and drop of blocks is in the WYSIWYG editor (the ⠿ handle beside a
block).

## Open a note as an outline

**Open note as outline** in the palette turns on fold toggles beside
headings and list items and folds everything to the top level — a note from
Logseq, made of nested `- ` items, opens as an outline you can expand step
by step. Run it again to turn it off. It is remembered for each note.

## Nothing goes into the file

Folding and zoom only change what you see. The note is byte-for-byte the
same after folding, zooming and unfolding. Which blocks are folded is kept
for each note in the browser (localStorage), not in the file, so the file
reads the same in every other editor and in Git. A section folded in one
editor is folded in the other.

pages.title: Pasting from Word, Google Docs and the web
pages.description: Paste from Word, Google Docs, Wikipedia, news sites or Gmail, in Hebrew or English, and get clean Markdown that keeps the structure and drops the styling.
pages.md:
Most text reaches a note by pasting. Lumen turns what the clipboard holds
into clean Markdown, in both editors.

## What is kept

- Headings, including Word's Title and Heading styles.
- Bulleted and numbered lists, nested lists included. Word and Google Docs
  write lists in their own ways (Word as indented paragraphs, Docs as one
  flat list per level), and Lumen rebuilds them as real nested lists.
- Tables, with each cell's bold, links and line breaks.
- Links and images.
- Bold, italic, strikethrough and code. Google Docs marks these with
  styles, not tags, and Lumen reads the styles.
- Quotes, including the quoted reply in a Gmail message.

## What is dropped

- Every inline style: fonts, sizes, colours, margins and alignment. A note
  never gets `style=` from a paste.
- Direction attributes (`dir`). Each paragraph finds its own direction, so a
  Hebrew paragraph sits on the right and an English one on the left.
- Invisible direction characters (LRE, RLE, PDF, LRO, RLO, the isolates, and
  doubled marks). An LRM or RLM is kept only where it decides the order of
  the text right after it, such as `שלום‎ (2)`.
- Site clutter: scripts, forms, Wikipedia's edit links and citation
  markers, and email signatures.

## Two ways to paste

| | Source editor | WYSIWYG |
|---|---|---|
| **Ctrl+V / ⌘V** | HTML with structure becomes Markdown. Code copied from a code editor stays plain text. | The cleaned HTML becomes headings, lists and tables. |
| **Paste as plain text** (command palette) | The clipboard's text, as is | The clipboard's text, as is |
| **Paste with formatting** (command palette) | Always converts the HTML | Always converts the HTML |

The palette commands read the clipboard, so the browser may ask for
permission the first time.

## Tested

Thirty clipboard samples are converted on every test run, each checked
against its expected Markdown. They cover Word, Google Docs, Wikipedia
(English and Hebrew), a Hebrew news site and Gmail, in Hebrew, English and
mixed text. The run also checks for zero inline styles and zero needless
direction marks.

A second set is a real corpus (`src/__tests__/fixtures/real-corpus`): the
same thirty Hebrew-first documents as Google Docs and Word put them on the
clipboard, as LibreOffice Writer does, and as the text a PDF reader copies
(pdf.js and poppler) out of the PDF LibreOffice printed. All 150 paste
whole: headings, nested lists, tables, links, images and right-to-left
text. Text pasted from a PDF reader loses the invisible direction
embeddings some readers add to each line.

pages.title: Hebrew pasted from a PDF
pages.description: Hebrew copied out of a PDF often comes out backwards or with the wrong final letters. Lumen notices and offers the fix.
pages.md:
Copy a paragraph out of a Hebrew court ruling, government form or article in
PDF, paste it into a note, and it often reads backwards:

```
2024 תנשב PDF-ה ץבוק
```

That is the order the PDF **drew** the letters, left to right, not the order
you read them. Some PDFs also mix up the final letters, giving `שלומ`
instead of `שלום`, or `םשרד` instead of `משרד`.

## The suggestion after a paste

Lumen pastes exactly what was on the clipboard. Then, if the text looks like
reversed Hebrew or Hebrew with broken final letters, a message offers the fix:

> **Looks reversed — fix?**
> Preview: קובץ ה-PDF בשנת 2024

**Fix** replaces exactly what you pasted, as one change, so **Ctrl+Z** brings
the original back. If you ignore the message, nothing changes. This works in
the source editor and in WYSIWYG.

For text that is already in a note, select it and run **Fix reversed Hebrew
(from a PDF)** from the command palette (⌘K).

## What the fix does

- **Reverses each line into reading order.** Lines stay in their order.
- **Keeps numbers, English words and links the right way round.**
  `03-1234567`, `GPT-4`, `gov.il` and `Smith et al. (2021)` are left as they
  are.
- **Turns brackets back the right way.** In a PDF, a bracket inside Hebrew is
  drawn as its mirror image.
- **Fixes final letters.** The last letter of a word gets its final form, and
  a final form inside a word gets its regular one. Acronyms such as
  `מ״מ` or `בג״ץ`, and prefixes before a hyphen such as `כ-35%`, are left alone.

## How it decides

Correct Hebrew never has a final letter at the start of a word (`םולש`), a
common word spelled backwards (`לש`, `אוה`, `ןיב`), or a sentence that
starts with its full stop. Lumen looks for these signs. If the text also
shows signs of reading forwards, such as final letters at word ends or
common words spelled the right way, it does not suggest a fix.

The same check runs over every Hebrew string in Lumen's own interface, more
than 1,400 of them, and finds nothing to fix.

## Limits

- **A line made of one word and a number** may not have enough to go on. An
  example is `טלפונ: 03-1234567`. When the signs are too weak, no fix is
  suggested, and you can still select the text and run the command.
- **A single word ending in a regular letter is left alone,** because it may
  be a loanword (`טיפ`).
- **Some PDF readers put words in reading order but the runs in the wrong
  order.** For example, `PDF קובץ ה-` instead of `קובץ ה-PDF`. That kind of
  copy is not detected.

The same check runs over every Hebrew string in Lumen's own interface, more than 1,400 of them, and finds nothing to fix.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text: A line made of one word and a number may not have enough to go on. An example is טלפונ: 03-1234567. When the signs are too weak, no fix is suggested, and you can still select the text and run the command. A single word ending in a regular letter is left alone, because it may be a loanword (טיפ). Some PDF readers put words in reading order but the runs in the wrong order. For example, PDF קובץ ה- instead of קובץ ה-PDF. That kind of copy is not detected.

pages.description: Niqqud for reading that never changes the note, a dyslexia-friendly layout, and read-aloud that highlights each word.
pages.md:
Open the command palette (**⌘K / Ctrl+K**) and run **Reading aids…**. Everything here
changes how a note *looks or sounds*; nothing here changes the note or its file.

## Show niqqud (display only)

**Show niqqud (display only)** — in the palette, or the first switch in Reading aids —
adds vowel points to the Hebrew in the preview, for reading. The note, the editor and
the file on disk stay byte for byte as written (a test checks the bytes before and after).

- Niqqud is added **on this device** by the Nakdimon model (MIT), the same one as
  **Add niqqud**. It asks before downloading the model the first time.
- Code, keyboard keys, math, text marked `data-no-nikud` and any editable surface (the
  WYSIWYG editor) are never pointed. Text you pointed yourself keeps your niqqud.
- A result that would change a letter is never shown: only the same letters with marks
  added.
- It lasts for this session; run the command again to hide it. To write niqqud into the
  note, use **Add niqqud** instead.

## Dyslexia-friendly layout

Turn on **Use the dyslexia-friendly layout**. It applies to the preview and to the
editor's text, and is remembered on this device.

| Setting | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Letter spacing | 0.12 em | Extra letter spacing helped dyslexic children read faster and more accurately (Zorzi et al., *PNAS* 2012). 0.12 em is the WCAG 2.2 text-spacing value (SC 1.4.12). |
| Word spacing | 0.16 em | WCAG 1.4.12; the British Dyslexia Association style guide asks for wide word spacing. |
| Line spacing | 1.8 | The BDA guide asks for at least 1.5. |
| Line focus | on | The paragraph under the pointer or the line with the cursor is highlighted, with a bar at its start as well as a colour. |
| Page colour | cream | The BDA guide recommends off-white or pastel backgrounds. Every tint keeps body text at 7:1 contrast or more, light and dark. |

### Fonts

| Choice | Hebrew | Latin | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|
| The app's font | Heebo | Inter | OFL 1.1 |
| Noto Sans Hebrew (default) | Noto Sans Hebrew | the app's | OFL 1.1 |
| OpenDyslexic | Noto Sans Hebrew | OpenDyslexic | OFL 1.1 (Reserved Font Name) |

There is no openly licensed font made for dyslexic readers of Hebrew, so the default is a
plain sans-serif with distinct letter shapes whose marks sit where they belong.
OpenDyslexic has no Hebrew letters; it is offered for Latin text because some readers
prefer it, though studies did not find it faster than a plain sans-serif (Wery &
Diliberto 2017; Kuster et al. 2018). The faces are downloaded from Lumen's own site when
you first choose them (never from a font service), then work offline.

## Read aloud with the word highlighted

**Read aloud** reads the note with your system's voices — on macOS, Windows, iOS and
Android that includes Hebrew. The sentence being read is highlighted in the editor, and
inside it **the word being spoken**, with an underline as well as a colour. Set the speed
in Reading aids.

- Only voices that run on this device are used, unless you allowed network voices (and
  never under the local-only AI policy).
- Word highlighting needs a voice that reports word boundaries. Most system voices do; if
  yours does not, only the sentence is highlighted.

## Not verified yet

The plan asks for a reading test with three readers with dyslexia (W4.25): reading speed
with the aids on must be the same or faster. That test has not been run yet.

pages.title: Reading options and Hebrew fonts
pages.description: Choose the Hebrew font, size, line height and column width of the preview — for every note or one note — with spaced Hebrew and a dyslexia-friendly font for English. Fonts download only when chosen, from the app itself.
pages.md:
**View → Reading options…** (or the command palette) sets how the preview
reads.

- **Apply to**: every note, or this note only. A note with its own settings
  keeps them when it is renamed. Choosing "every note" again drops them.
- **Hebrew font**: the app's own font, Heebo, Frank Ruhl Libre, Noto Sans
  Hebrew, Noto Serif Hebrew, Assistant or David Libre. A sample verse with
  nikud and cantillation marks shows the font before you read with it.
- **Text size, line height, column width**.
- **Spaced Hebrew**: more room between words and letters, and taller lines
  so that nikud above and below has room.
- **Dyslexia-friendly font for English text** (OpenDyslexic). It applies to
  Latin letters only; Hebrew keeps its own font.

## Privacy, size and offline

| Font | Licence | Download |
|---|---|---|
| Heebo, Frank Ruhl Libre | SIL OFL 1.1 | none (the app's interface fonts) |
| Noto Sans Hebrew | SIL OFL 1.1 | 29 KB |
| Noto Serif Hebrew | SIL OFL 1.1 | 32 KB |
| Assistant | SIL OFL 1.1 | 25 KB |
| David Libre | SIL OFL 1.1 | 50 KB (regular + bold) |
| OpenDyslexic | SIL OFL 1.1 | 207 KB (regular + bold) |

- No font is in the startup bundle or the offline precache. A font is
  downloaded the first time you choose it, from the app's own address and
  never from a font service, so no third party learns what you read. After
  that it is cached and works offline.
- All of them together are 0.34 MB of WOFF2 (the budget is 1.5 MB).
- The Hebrew files are subsets: Hebrew with every point and cantillation
  mark, the presentation forms, Latin-1 and punctuation, with every OpenType
  layout feature kept. `scripts/reading-fonts.sh` rebuilds them from
  upstream.
- OpenDyslexic has a Reserved Font Name, so its files are the upstream ones,
  unchanged. The licences are in `public/fonts/reading/OFL-*.txt`.

## Nikud

Nikud stays in place only when the font positions each mark against each
letter (OpenType mark-to-base anchors); otherwise vowels collide with the
letter or with each other. `src/__tests__/readingFonts.test.ts` reads each of
the five fonts (Noto Sans and Serif Hebrew, Frank Ruhl Libre, Assistant,
David Libre) and checks that every point is anchored to every letter that
takes points. `e2e/reading-fonts.spec.ts` renders a verse in every font and
attaches the pictures for a visual check.

## Limits

- Assistant, David Libre and Heebo have no meteg (U+05BD); the browser draws
  it from the next font in the list.
- Frank Ruhl Libre has no mark anchors on final mem, nun and tsadi (ם ן ץ),
  which take no points in standard Hebrew.
- OpenDyslexic has no Hebrew letters, which is why it applies to English
  text only.

pages.description: The Hebrew screen-reader journey run by Guidepup under VoiceOver and NVDA, and the accessibility-tree snapshots that run with every end-to-end test.
pages.md:
Automated checks such as axe find only part of what blocks a screen reader
user. Lumen checks screen-reader output at two levels.

## 1. Accessibility-tree snapshots (every e2e run)

`e2e/aria-hebrew.spec.ts` pins what a screen reader receives in the Hebrew
interface: roles, names and states. It uses Playwright's aria snapshots on
Chromium, with no screen reader needed:

- the skip link comes before the main landmark;
- a note's headings carry their levels, task checkboxes their state, and links their names;
- the command palette is a named modal dialog with a search box and results as options;
- the keyboard-shortcuts dialog is named and has a heading.

```sh
npx playwright test e2e/aria-hebrew.spec.ts --project=chromium
```

## 2. Real screen readers (Guidepup, on a Mac or Windows)

`sr/` runs ten tasks of the screen reader protocol (plan W1.23)
with [Guidepup](https://www.guidepup.dev/) (MIT). Guidepup drives VoiceOver
or NVDA and records what it says. Each task passes when the Hebrew it must
hear was spoken. The tasks are in `sr/journey.ts`.

Guidepup needs a real desktop: it takes over the screen reader, the keyboard
and the audio. It does not run in CI containers or in the cloud sandbox.

### On a Mac (VoiceOver)

```sh
npm install -D @guidepup/guidepup @guidepup/playwright @guidepup/setup   # once
npx @guidepup/setup                                       # once: lets VoiceOver be scripted
npm run test:sr -- --project=voiceover
```

Set the VoiceOver voice to Carmit (Hebrew) in VoiceOver Utility first.

### On Windows or a Windows VM (NVDA)

```sh
npm install -D @guidepup/guidepup @guidepup/playwright   # once
npx @guidepup/setup                                       # once: installs a portable NVDA
npm run test:sr -- --project=nvda-chrome
npm run test:sr -- --project=nvda-firefox
```

Set NVDA's voice to a Hebrew one (eSpeak NG Hebrew or Microsoft Asaf).

### Every night on the Mac

Once the three `@guidepup/*` packages are installed, `npm run nightly` on
the Mac (plan W4.36, [the nightly runs](/contributing/nightly/)) adds the
**sr** kind: `npx @guidepup/setup --ci`, then the VoiceOver journey. The
sealed report `reports/nightly/<date>-sr.json` holds, per setup, the tasks
passed, each blocker and the protocol row. `npm run nightly -- --only sr`
runs it alone.

The nightly needs the Mac logged in (VoiceOver speaks only in a user
session) with the screen unlocked. If System Integrity Protection is on,
`@guidepup/setup` can't write the permission itself: once, in System
Settings → Privacy & Security, give the terminal that runs the nightly
**Accessibility** and **Automation → VoiceOver**, and in VoiceOver Utility
turn on **Allow VoiceOver to be controlled with AppleScript**.

### Results

Each run prints a row for the protocol's results table, for example
`| 2026-11-12 | 0.1.0 | NVDA / Windows / chromium (Guidepup) | 10/10 (…) | — |`.
It also writes `sr-results/results.json`, with every phrase spoken in each
task. Paste the row into the protocol's results table and update the
accessibility conformance report from it. TalkBack stays a manual check,
once per release.

pages.md:
Automated checks such as axe find only part of what blocks a screen reader
user. This journey is run by a person, **without looking at the screen**,
with each screen reader, in **Hebrew** (Hebrew interface, Hebrew voice).
A step passes when it is done with the screen reader alone. A **blocker** is
a step that cannot be done at all. The release target is **0 blockers**
on every screen reader.

## Setups

| Screen reader | System | Browser | Voice |
|---|---|---|---|
| NVDA 2025.x | Windows 11 | Firefox and Chrome | eSpeak NG or Microsoft Asaf (Hebrew) |
| VoiceOver | macOS 15+ | Safari | Carmit (Hebrew) |
| VoiceOver | iOS 18+ | Safari | Carmit (Hebrew) |
| TalkBack | Android 14+ | Chrome | Google TTS, Hebrew |

Before starting: in Lumen, set the language to עברית (Settings → Language,
or the setup) and clear the site data so the first run starts fresh.

## The journey

1. **Start.** Open the app. The page title and the editor's name are read.
2. **Skip link.** Tab once: "Skip to the editor" is read; Enter moves focus into the editor.
3. **Write.** Type `# תוכנית`, Enter, then a line of Hebrew text. The text is read as typed, in Hebrew.
4. **Structure.** Arrow up to the first line: "כותרת 1: תוכנית" is read.
5. **Task.** Add `- [ ] לקנות חלב`, arrow away and back: "משימה, לא בוצעה" is read.
6. **Where am I.** Open the palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K), type `מיקום`, Enter: the line, the column and the heading are read.
7. **Palette.** In the palette, arrow through the results: each command's name is read, and the number of results is read when it changes.
8. **Dialog.** Open the keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+/ / ⌘/). The dialog's name is read, Tab stays inside, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the editor.
9. **Search.** Open search, type a word from the note, open the result: the note opens and focus is in the editor.
10. **Sidebar.** Open the workspace sidebar from the palette, move through the files and open one.
11. **Preview.** Switch to preview (from the palette). Headings can be listed with the screen reader's headings list, in order.
12. **AI.** If AI is set up: run a writing command. "ה-AI עובד…" and then "ה-AI סיים." are read, and the result can be reached.
13. **Mixed direction.** A line with Hebrew and an English word is read in the right order.
14. **Settings.** Open theme settings, switch to dark mode and back with the keyboard. Each control's state is read.

## Results

Each run adds a row: the date, the Lumen version, the setup, the steps that
passed, and each blocker with a link to its issue.

| Date | Version | Setup | Passed | Blockers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | 0.1.0 | NVDA / Windows | not run yet | — |
| — | 0.1.0 | VoiceOver / macOS | not run yet | — |
| — | 0.1.0 | VoiceOver / iOS | not run yet | — |
| — | 0.1.0 | TalkBack / Android | not run yet | — |

pages.title: Testing with screen reader users
pages.description: The kit for sessions with three Hebrew screen reader users — who to ask, the invitation, consent, the tasks, how a session is scored, and what happens to each barrier.
pages.md:
axe and the scripted readers find only part of what blocks people. Israeli
Standard 5568 is about real use, so before a release the
[screen reader protocol](/editor/screen-reader-protocol/) is also done by
**three people who use a screen reader every day, in Hebrew**. This page is
the kit for those sessions. The project owner recruits and runs them.

## Who

Three participants, one per setup, so every common reader is covered:

| Participant | Screen reader | System |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | NVDA (or JAWS) | Windows, Chrome or Firefox |
| 2 | VoiceOver | macOS or iPhone, Safari |
| 3 | TalkBack | Android, Chrome |

Each one uses the screen reader daily for at least a year and reads Hebrew
with it. No experience with Lumen or with Markdown is needed: the session
explains the four Markdown marks it uses.

## Organisations to ask

These Israeli organisations work with blind and low-vision people and with
digital accessibility. Ask them to pass the invitation on. Don't ask them
for anyone's contact details.

- **Migdal Or** (מגדלור), rehabilitation centre for the blind. It runs a
  national technology helpline staffed by blind and low-vision specialists,
  and accessibility checks for employers.
- **The Center for the Blind in Israel** (המרכז לעיוור בישראל).
- **Access Israel** (נגישות ישראל), aisrael.org. It runs usability testing
  with people with disabilities.
- **The Central Library for the Blind, Visually Impaired and Handicapped**,
  clfb.org.il. Its readers are experienced screen reader users.

## Compensation

A token payment, a gift card of 150–250 ₪ for a session of about an hour,
or a donation in the participant's name to one of the organisations above.
Volunteering is also fine if the participant prefers it. Say which in the
invitation.

## The invitation

> Lumen is a free, open-source note editor that works in Hebrew and runs on
> your own device. We're looking for three people who use NVDA, JAWS,
> VoiceOver or TalkBack every day, in Hebrew, for a one-hour session (online
> or in person). You'll do ten everyday tasks, like writing a note,
> finding one and changing a setting, while thinking aloud. We're testing
> the app, not you. Every barrier you hit will be fixed before the next
> release. [Payment: gift card of ___ ₪ / donation / volunteer.] Reply to
> ___ to take part.

## Consent

Before the session, read this to the participant and note their answer:

- Taking part is voluntary. They can stop at any time without giving a
  reason, and still receive the payment.
- With their permission, the screen and the screen reader's speech are
  recorded. The recording is used only to fix barriers and is deleted
  within 90 days. Without permission, only written notes are kept.
- Their name is not published. The results table shows the setup only.

## The session

Use the 14 steps of the [screen reader protocol](/editor/screen-reader-protocol/).
Pick the 10 everyday ones: steps 1–9 and 14. Give each task in words, not
key names. Example: "Write a note called תוכנית with a heading and one task".
Then wait.

For each task, write down:

- **done** (alone), **done with a hint**, or **not done** (a **blocker**)
- what the participant expected and what the reader said instead

A session passes when the participant completes **8 or more of the 10**

pages.md:
Open **Settings** from the command palette (`⌘K` → *Settings*). Every
older settings dialog now opens here, on its own tab:

| Tab | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| General | View mode, theme, language, text direction, panels, editor switches (Vim, typewriter, spelling, grammar, TypeScript checks, suggesting), auto-save, daily writing goal, local AI, error reports |
| Theme | Accent color, fonts, size, line height, content width, presets |
| AI settings | AI policy and cost mode, who runs the agents, Ollama address and model, the model manager (downloads, storage), local grammar and research services, writing style |
| Collaboration settings | Signaling server, public signaling fallback, persistent server and its token |
| Train AI on my style | Fine-tuned model and whether AI requests use it |
| Trusted signing keys | The Ed25519 keys plugins must be signed with |
| Organization | Name, allowed email domains, SSO, audit log |

## Search

Type in the search box at the top. Lumen matches the name of every
setting — including the ones inside a tab, such as *Ollama* or
*signaling* — and shows only the tabs that have a match. In the General
tab, only the matching settings stay on screen.

## Export and import

**Export JSON** downloads `lumen-settings.json` with your choices. It never
contains:

- API keys, tokens or passwords;
- your notes, open tabs, caches or history;
- the trusted plugin-signing keys or the organization policy.

**Import JSON** reads such a file back. Each value is checked against the
settings table: an unknown name, a secret, or a value of the wrong type is
skipped, and the toast tells you how many settings were imported and how
many were skipped. An import never loosens the AI policy: a file that says
*Cloud* doesn't move a device that keeps AI on this device to the cloud —
change that yourself in the AI tab.

## For developers

Every stored key and every persisted store field is listed in
`src/settings/schema.ts`, with its kind (`setting`, `secret` or `data`),
its tab and its label. `src/__tests__/settingsSchema.test.ts` scans the
sources and fails when a new key is missing from the table, so the screen,
its search and its export can't fall behind.

pages.title: Smart Insert (⌘⇧V)
pages.description: Paste anything into one dialog — Lumen detects the type and wraps it in the right block.
pages.md:
`⌘⇧V` opens a single dialog with one big text area. Paste **anything**
and Lumen figures out what to do with it — across 19 detectors, from
specific (a YouTube URL) to general (a code block whose language is
sniffed from the content).

## The detectors, in order

| Order | Match | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | YouTube / Vimeo / Spotify / Twitter / TikTok / Reddit / GitHub Gist / Figma / Maps / 8 more | ` ```embed ` |
| 2 | Bare HTTPS URL on a single line | Markdown link `[url](url)` |
| 3 | `$$…$$` or `\begin{equation}…\end{equation}` | Math fence |
| 4 | `flowchart LR …`, `sequenceDiagram`, `gantt`, … | ` ```mermaid ` |
| 5 | `digraph G { … }` | ` ```dot ` |
| 6 | `@startuml … @enduml` | ` ```plantuml ` |
| 7 | `X:1 T:Test K:C …` (ABC notation) | ` ```abc ` |
| 8 | `@article{…}` | ` ```bibtex ` |
| 9 | `{ "type": "FeatureCollection", … }` | ` ```map ` (GeoJSON) |
| 10 | YAML with `view:` + `type:` / `source:` | ` ```database ` |
| 11 | YAML with `series:` + `xAxis:` | ` ```chart ` |
| 12 | `CREATE TABLE / INSERT INTO / SELECT …` | ` ```sql ` (parsed to table) |
| 13 | JSON array of homogeneous objects | ` ```json-table ` |
| 14 | Other valid JSON | ` ```json ` |
| 15 | HTML with `<script>` / `<svg>` / `<canvas>` | ` ```htmlpreview ` (interactive iframe) |
| 16 | Other static HTML | Converted to markdown |
| 17 | `name,age\nalice,30\n…` | ` ```csv ` (table + chart suggestions) |
| 18 | Tab-separated rows | ` ```tsv ` |
| 19 | Code that sniffs as JS / TS / Python / Rust / Go / Java / C / C++ / PHP / Ruby / Dockerfile | ` ```<lang> ` |
| 20 | Anything else | Plain markdown — inserted as-is |

The first match wins. The detection badge in the dialog shows you
exactly what was identified ("Detected as: 🔗 YouTube embed") and a
dropdown lets you override.

## The preview pane

The dialog renders the converted markdown in a preview area below the
input. Live-updates as you type. You see exactly what's about to land
in the doc before you commit with ⌘↵.

## Insert position

- **At cursor** — uses the editor's exposed `insertText` handle so the
  surrounding selection is replaced cleanly.
- **Append** — adds to the end of the doc with two newlines.
- **Replace** — swaps the entire doc (use sparingly).

## Examples

> Paste "https://twitter.com/elonmusk/status/1585841080431321088"

→ Detected as: 🐦 X / Twitter embed → wraps as ```` ```embed ````.

> Paste "name,age\\nalice,30\\nbob,25"

→ Detected as: 📊 CSV table → wraps as ```` ```csv ```` and Lumen
suggests a bar chart based on the column types.

> Paste a multi-line `function fetch(url) { … }`

→ Detected as: 💻 JS code → wraps as ```` ```js ```` with Shiki
highlighting.

## Keyboard shortcut

`⌘⇧V` everywhere. Also reachable via:

- The toolbar's **Insert** menu → first item, marked with ✨.
- The command palette (`⌘K`), search "insert anything".

pages.title: Themes and CSS snippets
pages.description: Five built-in themes, among them one for Hebrew reading, theme files on the documented tokens, and CSS snippets from the vault that can never reach the network.
pages.md:
**Settings → Theme** (command palette: *Theme settings*) changes how Lumen
looks, live, without a reload: a theme switch takes one frame.

## Built-in themes

| Theme | For |
|---|---|
| Default | Lumen's own light and dark palette |
| Sepia | warm paper, low glare |
| Nord | cool blue-grey |
| High contrast | black on white and white on black, text at 7:1 |
| **Ktav (Hebrew reading)** | paper and ink, a Hebrew serif in the editor and the preview, more space between lines |

Every theme passes WCAG AA in both light and dark mode: body and muted text
at 4.5:1 or more against the background, the accent at 3:1, and text on the
accent at 4.5:1. The **Contrast** section of the settings shows the numbers
for what you have chosen, including your own accent colour.

**Ktav** sets the editor and the preview to a Hebrew serif that ships with
the system (Frank Ruehl CLM, David, Noto Serif Hebrew, then Times New
Roman), 16 px, with a line height of 1.85 and a 70-character measure. You
can change any of these after choosing the theme.

## Theme files and the tokens

**Export** saves your theme as JSON; **Import** reads one back, strictly
validated (8 KB at most, unknown keys refused). A theme only sets the
documented tokens: the custom properties below, consumed as
`hsl(var(--token))`.

| Token | Is |
|---|---|
| `--bg`, `--bg-subtle`, `--bg-muted`, `--bg-inset` | backgrounds, from the page to inset wells |
| `--fg`, `--fg-subtle`, `--fg-muted` | text, from body text to hints |
| `--border`, `--border-strong` | lines |
| `--accent`, `--accent-fg` | links, focus, buttons; text on the accent |
| `--editor-font`, `--editor-font-size`, `--editor-line-height` | the editor's type |
| `--content-width`, `--preview-width` | the measure of the editor and the preview |
| `--font-serif`, `--preview-line-height` | the preview's type (set by Ktav) |

The design system's other tokens — spacing, radii, shadows, motion — are
listed in *Contributing → Design system*; snippets can use them too.

## CSS snippets

Put `.css` files in the vault's `.lumen/snippets/` folder (Lumen also reads
`.obsidian/snippets/`, so a vault from Obsidian keeps its snippets). Each one
appears under **CSS snippets** in the theme settings with a switch. Changes
to the files apply as you save them.

Snippets can restyle anything, but **they can't load anything from the
network**. Before a snippet reaches the page, Lumen reads it the way the
browser does and removes:

- every `@import`;
- any declaration with `url()`, `image-set()`, `image()`, `cross-fade()`,
  `element()` or `attr(… url)` pointing anywhere but a `data:` image or font
  or a `#fragment`. That holds however it is written: `URL(`, `u\72l(`, quoted or
  not, inside a custom property or a `var()` fallback;
- old script hooks (`expression()`, `behavior`, `-moz-binding`) and
  `@document`.

The settings list what was removed, with the line and the reason. The
page's Content Security Policy is a second line, but on its own it would
allow a stylesheet to load images from any HTTPS site, so the sanitizer is
what keeps snippets off the network. As a third line, Lumen watches for any
request a stylesheet makes to another site, and the **privacy ledger**
would show it. Its tests check that a snippet full of remote URLs makes no
request at all.

pages.md:
Each of these has a **?** button that opens this help at its own section.

## Theme settings

**Theme settings…** in the command palette changes the colours, the
accent, the editor's font, size and line height, and the width of the
text, live. The **Contrast** section shows whether the text and the
accent are readable against the background. **Export** saves the theme as a
file and **Import** reads one back.

## Voice memos and dictation

Speak instead of typing. The quick mode writes what you say straight into
the note with the browser's speech recognition. The memo mode records the
audio, turns it into text and a summary, and inserts them as a voice-memo
block. Under the local-only AI policy this runs on your device; nothing is
sent anywhere. A pill at the bottom shows that the microphone is on; its
stop button ends the recording.

## Canvas

A whiteboard beside your notes: sticky notes, text, shapes, arrows,
frames and images on an infinite canvas, with pan, zoom, undo and redo.
Each canvas is saved in the vault as a `.tldr` file and saved again as you
draw.

## Sync conflicts

When the same note changed on this device and in the cloud since the
last sync, Lumen shows both versions side by side. Changes that don't
overlap are merged for you; for each part that does, choose this device's
or the cloud's version. You can also keep one side as a whole, or cancel
and decide later.

## Dialogs

Questions and confirmations open as small dialogs. **Enter** confirms,
**Escape** cancels, and focus goes back to where it was.

pages.title: Touch and phones
pages.description: Using Lumen with a finger or a pen — dragging, touch targets, the notch and the outline sheet — and how each is tested.
pages.md:
Lumen works by touch on phones and tablets, in Hebrew and in English.

## Dragging

Everything that drags with a mouse also drags with a finger or a pen:

- **Blocks in the rich editor.** Touch a block to show its handle, press the
  handle, slide, and lift where the block should go.
- **Tabs.** Press and hold a tab for a moment (about 0.4 s) to pick it up,
  slide it along the strip and lift to drop it. A quick swipe still scrolls
  the tab strip.
- **The sidebar edge.** Drag it to make the sidebar narrower or wider.
- **The graph view.** Tap a note's dot to open it; a finger has a wider hit
  area than the cursor.
- **Menus.** The slash menu, the formatting bubble and the AI button react to
  a tap the same way as to a click, and a tap outside closes them.

## Touch targets

On touch screens every button in the title bar, the status bar, toolbars and
the tab strip is at least **44 × 44** points, the size Apple and Google
recommend. The block handle grows to the same size.

## The notch and the home indicator

On phones with a notch or rounded corners Lumen uses the whole screen and
keeps the title bar and the status bar out of the notch, the corners and the
home indicator.

## The outline on a phone

On a narrow screen the outline is a **bottom sheet** instead of a side panel.
Open it from the command palette (*View → Outline*); picking a heading jumps
there and closes the sheet, and the ✕ button closes it too. Closing the
sheet on a phone does not change the side-panel setting on a wider screen.

## How it is tested

`e2e/touch.spec.ts` runs the full journey on an **iPhone 14** and a
**Pixel 7** profile (viewport, pixel ratio, touch input and the mobile user
agent): the safe-area viewport, the 44-pixel check on every control, typing,
the outline sheet, reordering tabs by long press, moving a block by its
handle. Opening a graph node by tap (a finger's wider hit area, no hover
before the tap) is a unit test in `src/__tests__/GraphViewRender.test.tsx`. Both profiles run on Chromium; Safari's
own engine is not part of the local run.

- **🖼** inserts a photo or an image from your files, stored in the vault
  like a pasted image;
- **H** makes a heading (tap again for a smaller one), **B** bold, **•** a
  bulleted list, **[[** a link to another note: type a few letters of its
  name and pick it from the list;
- **↶** undoes; **⌄** hides the keyboard.

Each button is one step: one undo takes it back. The row is 44 points high
like every touch target, scrolls sideways when it is longer than the
screen, and in Hebrew starts at the right, with its arrows pointing the way
the text moves.

### Making it yours

Tap **⋯** at the end of the row (or run *Customize the mobile toolbar* from
the command palette) to add actions (italic, numbered list, tag, code,
quote, redo and more), remove them, and move them with the ↑ and ↓ buttons.
**Reset** brings back the default row.

## Swipes

- Swipe in from the **start edge** of the screen for the file list, and from
  the **end edge** for the outline. "Start" follows the language: in Hebrew
  the file list comes in from the right, in English from the left.
- Swipe a panel back towards its edge to close it.

Only a swipe that starts within about 28 pixels of the edge counts, so
selecting text and scrolling a wide table work as before.

## Long notes open for reading

On a phone, a note of 600 words or more opens in reading view, so it's
quick to open and you don't bring up the keyboard by accident. **Tap the
text** to start editing: the editor opens with the cursor on the line you
tapped. Links, checkboxes, buttons and embeds still do what they do. Turn
this off with *Phone: open long notes for reading* in the command palette.

## Fewer taps

Ten common actions, in taps from an open note (a swipe or picking from a
list counts as one; typing a name doesn't):

| Action | Lumen | Obsidian Mobile | In Lumen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Turn a line into a task | 1 | 1 | toolbar ☐ |
| Indent a list item | 1 | 1 | toolbar ⇥ |
| Outdent a list item | 1 | 1 | toolbar ⇤ |
| Link to another note | 2 | 2 | toolbar [[, pick the note |
| Insert a photo | 2 | 2 | toolbar 🖼, pick the photo |
| Make the line a heading | 1 | 2 | toolbar H |
| Bold a word | 2 | 2 | double-tap the word, toolbar B |
| Open the file list | 1 | 1 | swipe in from the start edge |
| Open the outline | 1 | 2 | swipe in from the end edge |
| Start editing a long note at a paragraph | 1 | 2 | tap the paragraph |

The Obsidian Mobile column is counted by hand from its default toolbar and
gestures; it has not yet been measured on a device.

## How it is tested

`e2e/touch.spec.ts` runs the full journey on an **iPhone 14** and a
**Pixel 7** profile (viewport, pixel ratio, touch input and the mobile user
agent): the safe-area viewport, the 44-pixel check on every control, typing,
the outline sheet, reordering tabs by long press, moving a block by its
handle. Opening a graph node by tap (a finger's wider hit area, no hover
before the tap) is a unit test in `src/__tests__/GraphViewRender.test.tsx`. Both profiles run on Chromium; Safari's
own engine is not part of the local run.

`e2e/mobile-native.spec.ts` runs the phone editing journey on the same two
profiles, in Hebrew: the toolbar above the editor and its actions, the
customize sheet, both edge swipes mirrored, a long note opening for reading
and a tap landing on its line, and the time from launch to the last note.
The toolbar's text actions, the swipe rules and the tap-count table are
unit tests in `src/__tests__/mobileNative.test.ts`.

pages.title: Widgets, Shortcuts and Siri
pages.description: A Lumen widget on the home screen, Siri and Spotlight on iPhone, App Shortcuts on Android, and "Add to inbox" from the Shortcuts app — plus the steps to build them.
pages.md:
Lumen is one tap away on the phone, in Hebrew and in English.

## On the home screen

The **Lumen widget** (iPhone and Android) has three buttons:

- **Search** opens search.
- **Quick note** opens the quick-capture box with the cursor in it.
- **Today** opens today's daily note.

The widget shows no note text. In Hebrew the buttons run right to left.

## Siri, Spotlight and Shortcuts (iPhone)

These work without setup. Say them to Siri, type them in Spotlight, or
find them in the Shortcuts app:

| Say or search | What happens |
|---|---|
| "Add to Lumen inbox" | Siri asks what to add and adds it to the end of `inbox.md`, without opening Lumen |
| "Quick note in Lumen" | opens the quick-capture box |
| "Voice note in Lumen" | opens the box, recording |
| "Search Lumen" | opens search (and, from Shortcuts, with your query) |
| "Today's Lumen note" | opens today's note |

In Hebrew: "הוסף לתיבת הלכידה של Lumen", "פתק מהיר ב-Lumen", "חפש
ב-Lumen" and so on.

*Add to inbox* works even when Lumen is closed. The text waits on the
phone, and the next time Lumen opens it lands in `inbox.md` with the time
you said it. Each line is added once, and nothing is lost if Lumen is
closed again first.

## App Shortcuts (Android)

Long-press the Lumen icon: **Quick note**, **Voice note**, **Search** and
**Today**. Drag one to the home screen to keep it there.

## Links for other apps

Every widget button and shortcut is a link, which other apps and
automations can use too:

| Link | What it does |
|---|---|
| `lumen://capture` | opens the quick-capture box |
| `lumen://capture?mode=voice` | opens the box, recording |
| `lumen://capture?text=…` | adds the text to the inbox |
| `lumen://new` | opens a new note |
| `lumen://search?q=…` | opens search with the query |
| `lumen://daily` | opens today's note |

## For maintainers: building them

The native parts follow one rule: they only forward a link or a queued
line to the app. What a link means is decided in
`src/mobile/nativeActions.ts`, which is tested
(`src/__tests__/widgets.test.ts`). The Android link helper is
`LumenActions.java`, plain Java checked with `javac`.

### iOS (Xcode)

The repository has the sources. These steps add them to the Xcode project
once:

1. `npm run build && npx cap sync ios`, then open `ios/App/App.xcworkspace`
   (or `App.xcodeproj` with Swift Package Manager).
2. **App target, new files:** File → Add Files to "App"… and select:
   - `App/LumenNative.swift` and `App/LumenIntents.swift`, with *Target:
     App* ticked;
   - `App/en.lproj` and `App/he.lproj` (`Localizable.strings`,
     `AppShortcuts.strings`).
3. **Localizations:** Project → Info → Localizations, add **Hebrew**.
4. **The widget extension:**
   - File → New → Target → **Widget Extension**. Name it `LumenWidgets`,
     untick *Include Configuration App Intent* and *Include Live Activity*,
     and choose *Activate* when asked.
   - Delete the Swift file Xcode generated. Add
     `LumenWidgets/LumenWidgets.swift` and
     `LumenWidgets/en.lproj` / `he.lproj` to the **LumenWidgets** target.
   - Set its deployment target to iOS 16 or later, and its bundle id to
     `com.lumen.editor.LumenWidgets`.
5. **Signing:** set the same team for the App and LumenWidgets targets
   (the accounts are in plan 15.7). No App Group or new capability is
   needed: the widget only opens links, and Siri's *Add to inbox* runs in
   the app's own process.
6. `Main.storyboard` already uses `MainViewController`, which registers the
   app's plugin. Check that its class shows *Module: App*.
7. Build and run on a device. Long-press the home screen → **+** →
   **Lumen** to add the widget.

### Android (Android Studio)

Everything is in the project already: the widget (`LumenWidgetProvider`,
`res/layout/widget_lumen.xml`, `res/xml/widget_lumen_info.xml`), App
Shortcuts (`res/xml/shortcuts.xml`), the `lumen://` intent filter, and the
plugin, which `MainActivity` registers.

1. `npm run build && npx cap sync android`, then open `android/` in
   Android Studio.
2. Build → Make Project, then run on a device or an emulator (API 26 or
   later).
3. Long-press the home screen → **Widgets** → **Lumen** to add the widget.
   Long-press the app icon for the shortcuts.

### Manual checks on real devices

The plan asks for these to be done and written down, on an iPhone and an
Android phone, with the phone in Hebrew and then in English:

1. **Tap → typing under 1 second:** record the screen at 60 fps, tap
   *Quick note* on the widget, and count frames from the tap to the
   blinking cursor. The app also logs `widget tap → typing` from the moment
   it receives the link, which leaves out the system's launch time.
2. **Siri:** say "Add to Lumen inbox" and then a sentence, with Lumen
   closed. Open Lumen: the sentence is at the end of `inbox.md`, with the
   time you said it.
3. **Shortcuts app:** make a shortcut with *Add to Lumen inbox* and run it.
   The same result.
4. **RTL:** with the phone in Hebrew, the widget buttons run right to left
   and the labels are in Hebrew. The same holds for the App Shortcuts.
5. **Each link:** `lumen://search?q=test` from the browser opens search
   with "test".

pages.title: Beta channel and feature flags
pages.description: Try new features before everyone else, on the web or in the desktop app, and turn any beta feature on or off on your own device.
pages.md:
New features reach a **beta** first, then a stable release after testing.

## The beta

- **On the web:** the beta is a separate site, built from the same code,
  with new features turned on. A **Beta** badge in the status bar shows you
  are on it. Your notes stay in your browser as usual: the beta and the
  stable site are separate origins and don't share storage. To move notes
  between them, keep the vault in a folder on disk and open that folder in
  both, or export from one and import into the other.
- **In the desktop app:** command palette → **Update channel: switch between stable and beta**. Beta also
  installs beta releases; stable installs only tested releases. If you go
  back to stable, you stay on your current version until a stable release
  is newer, because the app never installs an older version.

Betas are numbered like `0.2.0-beta.1`. Once a beta has been tested, the
same changes ship as `0.2.0`.

## Feature flags

Each feature in beta has a flag. Command palette → **Feature flags…**
(or tap the **Beta** badge) lists them:

- **On or off:** turn any flag on or off for yourself. In a stable build
  you can try a beta feature; in a beta build you can turn one off.
- **Where the value comes from:** *Default for this build*, or *Your
  choice*, with a link back to the default. **Reset all** clears your
  choices.
- **Private:** flags are local. Lumen doesn't fetch them from a server and
  doesn't report them anywhere. Your choices stay in this browser or app.

Features in beta now:

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| Check for updates at launch | Desktop app: looks for a new version once a day when Lumen starts, so beta fixes arrive quickly. Never in *local only* mode; every check is in the privacy log. |

## How a feature graduates

A feature ships first in a beta with its flag on. A later release promotes
the flag to stable, and the feature is on for everyone. The project's
release check refuses a flag that reaches stable without an earlier beta.

pages.title: The desktop app
pages.description: Windows, tabs you drag between them, the tray with quick capture, opening .md files from Finder or Explorer, and lumen:// links.
pages.md:
The desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux) works like a native one.

## Windows and tabs

- **New window:** *File → New window* (⌘⇧N / Ctrl+Shift+N), or *New
  window* in the command palette. Every window shows the same vault and
  keeps its own tabs.
- **Move a tab:** drag it out of the tab strip and drop it on another
  window. Drop it outside every window to get a new window with that tab.
  The tab keeps its editing state: unsaved text, cursor and selection,
  scroll position and view mode. Undo history starts fresh in the new
  window.
- The move is safe: the first window keeps the tab until the second one
  has it open. If the second window closes first, nothing is lost.
- When you close an extra window, its tabs close with it. The main window
  remembers its tabs for the next launch.

## The tray

The Lumen icon in the menu bar (macOS) or the system tray (Windows, Linux)
has:

- **Quick capture…:** a small window. Type a thought and press Enter, and
  it is added to `inbox.md` with the date and time. Shift+Enter starts a
  new line, and Esc closes the window.
- **New note**, your **recent notes**, **Show Lumen** and **Quit Lumen**.

The menu follows the app's language.

## Opening files

Lumen registers itself for **`.md`** (and `.markdown`), **`.base`**
(database views) and **`.excalidraw`** (drawings). Double-click one in
Finder, Explorer or your file manager, or use *Open with → Lumen*, or run
`lumen note.md` in a terminal:

- **A file inside a vault** opens in that vault. If it belongs to a vault
  you used before, Lumen switches to it first. With vaults inside each
  other, the innermost one wins.
- **A file outside every vault** opens on its own. Saving writes it back
  to the same file, and nothing else on the disk becomes reachable.
- If Lumen is already running, the file opens in the running app. A second
  copy of Lumen is not started.

## Links: `lumen://`

| Link | What it does |
|---|---|
| `lumen://open?path=notes/idea.md` | opens a note of the current vault |
| `lumen://open?path=notes/idea.md&vault=Research` | opens it in the vault whose folder is named *Research* |
| `lumen://open?path=notes/idea.md&line=12` | opens it with the cursor on line 12 |
| `lumen://new` | opens a new note |
| `lumen://new?title=Idea&text=First%20line&folder=inbox` | opens a new note with that title and text; it isn't saved until you save it |
| `lumen://capture?text=Buy%20milk` | adds a line to `inbox.md` |

Encode values as you would in a URL. Hebrew works: `lumen://open?path=%D7%A8%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%95%D7%9F.md`.

Links are checked strictly, because a link can come from anywhere:

- `path` is inside the vault: no `..`, no absolute path, no drive letter;
- `vault` matches only a vault you opened before; a link can never point
  Lumen at a new folder;
- `new` opens an unsaved note, so nothing is written that you haven't seen.

- link parsing, including every way to escape the vault;
- which vault holds a file, with nested vaults, `..`, and case on macOS and
  Windows;
- launch arguments;
- where a dropped tab lands, and the two-phase move (never lost, never
  doubled);
- the tray menu and quick-capture entries.

   scroll come along, and the first window no longer has the tab.
5. Tray → *Quick capture…* in Hebrew: the window is right to left, and
   Enter adds the line to the inbox.

pages.title: Desktop app updates
pages.description: How the Lumen desktop app checks for, verifies and installs updates, and what it sends.
pages.md:
The desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) updates itself from the project's
GitHub releases.

- **Check:** command palette → **Check for updates…**. A stable build never
  checks on its own. A beta build checks once a day at launch, unless you
  turn that off under [feature flags](/getting-started/beta/).
- **Channel:** command palette → **Update channel: switch between stable and beta** switches between stable
  and beta releases ([beta channel](/getting-started/beta/)).
- **What is sent:** one request to the release server with the app version
  and platform. No notes, no account, no identifier. It appears in the
  privacy log.
- **Local only:** when the privacy policy is *local only*, nothing is
  checked. The command says so instead.
- **Verification:** every update is signed. The app checks the signature
  against the key built into it and refuses a file that doesn't match, or an
  older version presented as new.
- **Install:** after you confirm, Lumen downloads, verifies, installs and restarts.

A build without the update key (local and development builds) has no
updater. *Check for updates…* says it isn't configured, and new versions are
installed by hand.

## Signed installers

Release installers are code-signed once the project's signing certificates
are in place (Windows Authenticode, Apple Developer ID). Until then Windows
SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper show a warning on first launch.

## What the app is allowed to do

The window has no general file-system permission. It reaches only the vault
folder you picked, through Lumen's own commands. No shell, no arbitrary
HTTP from the native side, and no source maps in the shipped files.

pages.title: Send feedback
pages.description: Report a bug, an idea or a question as a GitHub issue or as text to copy. Lumen has no feedback server, and nothing is sent until you click.
pages.md:
Open it with `⌘K → Help: Send feedback`, or with **Report a problem…** at the
bottom of the [AI doctor](/ai/doctor/).

Lumen has no feedback server. The form turns what you write into the text of
a GitHub issue, and you choose what happens to it:

- **Open on GitHub** opens github.com in a new tab with the issue form filled
  in (title, text and a label for the kind). You check it there and submit it.
  You need a GitHub account.
- **Copy text** puts the same text on your clipboard, for an e-mail or
  anywhere else.

Until you click one of those two buttons, nothing leaves your device. The form
makes no network request, and the preview shows exactly the text that will be
sent.

## What goes in

| Part | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| Kind, title, description | always | what you wrote |
| App and browser details | ticked (the default) | Lumen version; web, installed app or desktop; platform; language; AI policy; the browser's user agent |
| AI doctor report | only when you tick it | the doctor's checks of the local AI stack. It never contains note text. Keys, tokens, passwords in URLs and e-mail addresses are removed before it goes in. |
| Screenshot | only when you take one | never part of the text (see below) |

If the issue text is too long for a link, GitHub opens with the title only and
the text is on your clipboard: paste it into the issue.

## Screenshots

**Save a screenshot to attach** asks your browser to capture a screen, window or
tab. The browser shows its own prompt, so you choose what is captured. The
picture is saved on your computer as `lumen-feedback-<date>-<time>.png`. It is
not uploaded. Attach it to the GitHub issue yourself. It may show your notes,
so look at it first.

Browsers without screen capture (most phones) say so and skip this step.

## Diagnostics file

**Save diagnostics** (in the feedback form, on an error screen, or **Save a
diagnostics file** in the command palette) saves `lumen-diagnostics-<date>.json`
on your computer, for you to attach to the issue. It holds what a maintainer
needs to understand a problem, and nothing about what you wrote:

- the version, the app shell (web, installed, desktop), the platform and
  the browser;
- your settings, copied one by one from a fixed list: switches, modes and
  sizes. No note names, folders, keys, tokens or e-mail addresses;
- the vault counted, not read: how many notes, other files and folders, and
  their total size;
- storage: whether the vault is in the browser's private storage, and how
  full it is;
- the last warnings and errors, with every path, URL path, quoted text,
  address and key in them replaced by a placeholder.

Before the file is saved, Lumen checks it once more against the text it
holds in memory (your notes, their names, your keys), and refuses to save a
file that would contain any of it.

## Help in the app

**Help** in the command palette (or F1) opens this documentation inside
Lumen. It is packed into the app, so it works offline, and its search
handles Hebrew prefixes as the website's search does. Every panel and
dialog has a **?** button that opens the help at the part about it.

pages.description: Export Bear notes as Markdown and bring them, with their images, into Lumen.
pages.md:
## Export from Bear

1. Select the notes (or **⌘A** in a tag).
2. **File → Export Notes…**, format **Markdown**, with **Export attachments**
   on. Bear writes one `.md` file per note and a folder of images next to
   each.

## Bring it in

Zip the export folder, or keep it as a folder, then
`⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`. The notes and
their images go into a new folder, `Imported/<name>`, with the image links
intact.

## What changes

| In Bear | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| `#tags` and `#nested/tags` | the same inline tags; the tags panel lists them |
| `#multi word tags#` | write them as `#multi-word-tags` (Lumen tags have no spaces) |
| `::highlight::` | kept as text; Markdown has no highlight (use **bold**, or `{==highlight==}` in suggesting mode) |
| `[[note links]]` | the same syntax |
| Sync between devices | Bear's iCloud sync does not reach Lumen; use Git or a shared folder |

1. In Google Docs: **File → Download → Markdown (.md)**. Older documents

## Export from Notion

1. In Notion: **Settings → Export** (a single page: **⋯ → Export**).
2. Choose **Markdown & CSV**, include subpages, and download the .zip.
